look_here_first: CURLYMESQUITE / Hilaria belangeri: FIRST examine true inner 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule at an opened leaf blade–sheath junction, not hairs on a distant reddish culm node. SECOND inspect short terminal spikelike heads with 4–8 clustered units, and compare attached and detached papery reproductive parts. The project already has authentic mature heads and detached groups but no calibrated dissection confirming the individual central/lateral members. THIRD examine fine curly leaves, hairy stem nodes and existing photographed thin aboveground stolons. Only LATER pursue exposed roots at stolon nodes. Tobosa has similar grouped heads but coarser habit.

best_field_traits: Perennial short sod-forming grass with wiry aboveground creeping stolons; no rhizomes in the Hill Country vegetative treatment.
Stolon nodes can root, produce upright leafy tufts, and show conspicuous ringlike hairs.
Short erect culms around 10–30 cm in Hill Country specimens; new growth pale green, dried blades frequently curly.
Blades thin, often 1–3 mm wide in regional treatment, tending to curl when dry; blade shape alone insufficient.
Membranous true ligule ~0.5–1 mm long, obtuse/truncate and irregularly torn; avoid mixing it up with marginal collar hairs.
Flowering head a single short spike-like axis bearing tight groups of three spikelets. Falling fascicles leave zigzag-looking branch.
Variable flowering and seed set; vigorous vegetative spreading can persist with little conspicuous seed production.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole 10–30 cm patch in grassland with ruler.
One continuous aboveground wiry STOLON attached to rooted nodes/tufts; close-up of hairy node (high priority).
Leaf blade fresh versus same dried/curling tissue, with ruler.
True 0.5–1 mm ligule at collar with mm reference.
Full terminal spike with multiple triads; fascicle and exposed zigzag axis after detachment.
crew_field_check: Trace stems to base: does this grass use aboveground rooted stolons or buried scaly rhizomes?
Check collar true ligule under magnification, then one intact three-spikelet fascicle.
Never call a species from zigzag rachis or dry color alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Tobosa (H. mutica) has short, thick SCALY BELOWGROUND rhizomes and no creeping surface stolons, with taller 30–70 cm wiry culms and stiffer, often broader leaves. Both have spikelet fascicles and zigzag stems after seed fall, so the seedhead alone is not proof. Buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides) can form short turf but has distinct male and female flowering structures, and bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has a spoke-like digitate inflorescence (3–7 radiating spikes) rather than a solitary short Hilaria flowering axis.

field_matrix.spread: ABOVE-GROUND slender stolons rooting at hairy nodes
field_matrix.head: Single short terminal axis of three-spikelet fascicles

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: CURLYMESQUITE: a short perennial native lawnlike grass often 10–30 cm with little CURLING leaves when dry and relatively small terminal spike-like heads of grouped spikelets. Its best confirmation is a THIN WIRY ABOVEGROUND STOLON physically connecting tufts with hairy rooting nodes (connected aboveground runners NOW photographed in panel 8; node roots and the hair ring themselves still unproved). A short grouped head does NOT distinguish it from tobosa alone. Don't confuse with Bermuda's radiating finger spikes, buffalograss's separate male/female structures, or vine mesquite's long swollen nodes.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Tobosa (H. mutica) has short, thick SCALY BELOWGROUND rhizomes and no creeping surface stolons, with taller 30–70 cm wiry culms and stiffer, often broader leaves. Both have spikelet fascicles and zigzag stems after seed fall, so the seedhead alone is not proof. Buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides) can form short turf but has distinct male and female flowering structures, and bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has a spoke-like digitate inflorescence (3–7 radiating spikes) rather than a solitary short Hilaria flowering axis.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.title: Curlymesquite: inspect real ligule and flowering parts before tracing rooting stolons
photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: WIRY STOLON ROOTING ABOVE SOIL + SHORT CURLY TURF + GROUPED SPIKELETS.

steps.what: Compare whole field grass patch, generally far shorter than robust tobosa stands; grazing makes stature unreliable.

steps.look: Correct TRUE 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule, best with a scale
steps.what: Gently pull leaf blade back from sheath and photograph the short free membrane; white hairy node tufts in existing archived photo are a DIFFERENT stem feature, never a ligule. Species-specific true-ligule macro STILL MISSING.

steps.stage: 3 — INSPECT ATTACHED HEAD AND DETACHED SPIKELET GROUPS
steps.look: Single short spike-like axis with regularly grouped units
steps.what: Two source-verified Patrick Alexander CC0 original flowering anatomy photos and earlier head photographs are installed; label gross papery parts, not unproven fertile-vs-staminate boundaries.

steps.look: Narrow blades that often curl as they dry
steps.what: Inspect several live and dry blades with field closeup; rolling/curling is supporting evidence, not definitive.

steps.what: Pair observed surface stolon with actual species head and collar before an exact species identification.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Curlymesquite: real reproductive dissection → sheath/collar → actual rooted stolons
steps: LIGULE STILL INCOMPLETE: the Bob Harms original photograph labelled ligule/sheath truly shows the sheath and hair placement with size reference, but the FREE membrane edge is NOT clearly exposed. Gently open a verified specimen's INNER blade–sheath junction with 10–20× lens and millimeter scale before labelling the actual 0.5–1 mm membranous lacerate ligule.

NEXT inspect the Bob Harms labeled real black-background dissection: fertile floret, lemma, palea and caryopsis, sterile lemmas, and multiple full spikelet clusters. Read the original labels and ruler rather than guessing internal parts from a whole head.

Look at the separate real mature fascicles on black background: three separate whole photographed clusters are shown, each bearing papery expanding bracts. Don't confuse these with the three spikelets INSIDE one reproductive fascicle.

TRACK REPRODUCTIVE MATURITY: compare Patrick Alexander's genuine green tightly closed heads, purple flowering groups and old open pale dry units on real separate plants; colors change as reproductive bracts mature and shed.

LATER inspect Bob Harms' REAL lifted curlymesquite rooted tuft: fibrous roots emerge beneath a central leafy shoot, thin stolons link other shoots. Do NOT label an unseen root at the distant right-hand node.

COMPARE TO TOBOSA: use distinct source-labelled Hilaria mutica views. Tobosa is coarser, with stout underground scaly rhizomes; curlymesquite has thin visible ABOVEGROUND runner stolons. Use linked physical structures and measured spikelets, not one seedhead silhouette.

GROWTH STRUCTURE COMPARISON AFTER ABOVEGROUND ID: Bob Harms's clear real curlymesquite has aboveground running stolons and connected central basal roots; the last separately labelled OTHER-SPECIES Tobosa USDA 1939 photograph shows a bisected thick scaly UNDERGROUND rhizome area below the ruler. Both are source-identified true photos, but the dark historical Tobosa source cannot teach individual rhizome buds or root attachments.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Curlymesquite: low turf AND a demonstrated thin ABOVEGROUND stolon connecting tufts, with genuine hairy rooting nodes where soil is exposed, then a short Hilaria-type grouped head. Do not require fully rooted nodes to be visible in one archived reference photograph.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · OPEN THE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: True ligule is a 0.5–1 mm membrane
field_id_short_tiles.details: At the INNER blade–sheath junction, look for an actual short membranous ligule approximately 0.5–1 mm long (regional Texas flora/NPS treatment). Narrow blades are often 1–2(3) mm wide. White node hairs are not the ligule. Open the collar and use a 0.5-mm scale; archived gross views do not measure the membrane.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED 0.5–1 mm MEMBRANE — MEASURED PHOTO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · COUNT THE TRIADS
field_id_short_tiles.short: 4–8 three-spikelet groups on a short axis
field_id_short_tiles.details: A slender terminal spikelike head is commonly 2–3.5 cm long and carries about 4–8 groups of THREE spikelets. The CENTRAL spikelet has one fertile bisexual floret; TWO lateral spikelets are predominantly staminate, commonly two-flowered. Groups detach as units and may leave a zigzag rachis. These counts are from the Fort Worth/Texas regional treatment, not measured from archived JPEGs.
field_id_short_tiles.status: HEAD PHOTOS AVAILABLE; SEXED TRIAD DISSECTION MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE CENTRAL SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Glume awns are not lemma awns
field_id_short_tiles.details: A mature three-spikelet cluster is generally about 4.5–6 mm in the regional treatment. The central spikelet has basally united, often asymmetric glumes with awnlike extensions commonly 2.5–5 mm; the thin central fertile lemma is described as AWNLESS in the NPS treatment. Never label a glume projection as a fertile-lemma awn. Isolate both central glumes, lemma and palea before placing arrows.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LITERATURE ANATOMY; BRacts NOT SEPARATELY PHOTOGRAPHED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK THE OUTER SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two male companions surround the central fertile one
field_id_short_tiles.details: The two lateral spikelets of each cluster are male/staminate and commonly two-flowered, while the central member bears the seed-producing floret. Lateral glumes may be unequal and lobed; the central and lateral bracts must be photographed separately under a 1-mm ruler. Do not mistake the entire three-spikelet fascicle for a single multiflowered spikelet.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SEX AND BRAct SEPARATION NOT PIXEL-VERIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tobosa rhizomes below; curlymesquite runners above
field_id_short_tiles.details: Tobosa (Hilaria mutica) has a coarse perennial stand and short thick SCALY UNDERGROUND rhizomes, not the thin surface-rooting stolons of curlymesquite; both have compact triad-bearing heads. Vine mesquite (Hopia obtusa) has much longer stolons with swollen nodes but a different flowering architecture. Bermudagrass has fingerlike radiating spikes; buffalograss has distinct male and female flowering structures. Do not certify species from dry color or a lone head. Photograph the correct organ: nodal hair tufts on the CREEPING RUNNER, not hairs on the INNER blade/sheath COLLAR. Published regional treatments describe a short true membranous ligule, and some vegetative keys say the collar is largely glabrous.
field_id_short_tiles.status: COMPARISONS WRITTEN; MATCHED ROOTED PHOTOS NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · SURFACE-STOLON CONFIRMATION (LATER)
field_id_short_tiles.short: Creeping native turf: follow a wiry stolon
field_id_short_tiles.details: Curlymesquite is a low perennial, commonly 10–30 cm tall. Trace a slender ABOVEGROUND runner to a rooting node and a second leafy tuft; bearded nodes and narrow leaves that curl as they dry support the ID. A short compact head alone cannot distinguish it from tobosa. Panel 8 physically archives a real uninterrupted ABOVEGROUND stolon connecting a parent leaf tuft to daughter shoots; however its hair-ring and rooted soil node remain unproved.
field_id_short_tiles.status: KNOWN ABOVEGROUND STOLON PHOTO, ROOTING NODE STILL NEEDS PROOF — DEFERRED
